> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p-value<0.05", "p-value<0.05"), 
    Text = c("Genes with an FDR-adjusted p-value<0.05 were enriched with non-synonymous mutations and considered driver genes.", 
    "A p-value<0.05 or, when applicable, a padjusted value<0.05 was considered statistically significant."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p=0.25", Sentence = "At the genomic level, D/P tumors showed a higher burden of SV deletions than other subtypes (adjusted p=0.0045) and contained RB1 mutations in 7 of 19 (37%), although this enrichment was not statistically significant after multiple-testing correction (adjusted p=0.25) (Supplementary Figure 10)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Background: Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally.
Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival.
The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood.
A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies.

To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment.

Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations.
Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes.
Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA).
Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins.
text.formatted: Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins.

text.text: Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch . repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes.
The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2.
GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes.
Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation.
These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity.
WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features.
WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients.
Conclusions: CUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes.
Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior.
Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.

text.text: The clinical complexity, therapeutic uncertainty, and poor prognosis associated with CUP highlight the need for a deeper understanding of its biology.
Advances in molecular profiling technologies, particularly whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), offer opportunities to investigate CUP biology.
Although the underlying biological processes driving CUP tumorigenesis remain incompletely understood, multiple hypotheses have been proposed [7].

text.text: One hypothesis suggests that CUP represents metastasis from a conventional primary tumor that remains clinically occult because it is indistinguishable from metastatic disease, dormant, or regressed.

text.text: In this study, we characterized the genomic landscape of 283 CUP patients using WGS and identified driver genes and cancer hallmarks.

Overall, our integrated genomic and transcriptomic approach was designed to advance the understanding of CUP biology and support ongoing efforts to improve diagnosis and treatment for CUP patients.

text.text: Driver genes frequently altered by CNAs sCNAs identified by GISTIC2 were mapped to genes annotated in GENCODE (release 38) using the GRCh37 reference genome.

text.text: The input for GSVA was the VST-transformed gene expression matrix generated by DESeq2.
To subtype the CUP TME, we adopted an approach similar to that of Bagaev et al.
In short, a similarity matrix was constructed by calculating the Pearson's correlation coefficient between all CUP samples using the GSVA scores.
The matrix was then used to generate a weighted graph, where each node represented a sample and the edge weights corresponded to the Pearson's correlation values between pairs of samples.
Louvain clustering was subsequently applied to detect clusters within the graph using igraph R package[43] (v2.2.0).
To determine the optimal weight threshold for defining clusters, we checked the number of samples in each cluster.
Candidate thresholds that resulted in any cluster containing <5% of samples were excluded.

In this study, we interrogated and integrated whole-genome and transcriptomic sequencing data to characterize the genomic landscape, tumor microenvironment (TME), and potential therapeutic vulnerabilities of CUP.
Using WGS data from 283 patients, we identified mutational processes, recurrent driver alterations, structural variations (SVs), and putative genetic immune escape (GIE) events.
In a subset of 79 patients with matched RNA-seq data, transcriptomic subtyping revealed distinct immune-enriched/depleted, fibrotic, and proliferative TME states.

Together, these diverse findings further emphasized the marked heterogeneity of CUP and support the integration of genomic and transcriptomic data, in addition to tissue-of-origin (ToO) prediction, to better understand the biology of CUP.
Two predominant hypotheses have been proposed to explain CUP biology [54].
text.formatted: Two predominant hypotheses have been proposed to explain CUP biology <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[54]</ref>.

text.text: The first proposes that CUP represents metastasis arising from a conventional primary tumor that either cannot be distinguished from metastatic lesions or remains clinically occult, potentially due to early dissemination, dormancy or regression.
The second proposes that CUP is an independent entity lacking a conventional primary site counterpart.
Several observations in our data support the occult primary hypothesis in a substantial proportion of cases.
High-confidence CUPPA predictions were obtained for 58% of tumors, and many of these shared genomic characteristics with cancers with known primaries.

For example, tobacco-and UV-associated mutational signatures were linked to lung-and skin-like genomic profiles; TMPRSS2-ERG and FGFR2 fusions were detected in tumors with concordant CUPPA predictions; the enrichment of squamous/basaloid histology in the UV-signature group provided clinicopathological support for a cutaneous origin.

However, the remaining tumors assigned as "inconclusive" CUPPA predictions should not be interpreted as solid evidence for an independent CUP entity, as current classifiers are limited by the number and constellation of reference categories and features on which they are trained.
Additionally, previous work has shown that, no matter whether DNA-, RNA-or methylation-based, ToO approaches are only able to resolve a subset of clinicopathologically unresolved CUPs [10, 55].
text.formatted: Additionally, previous work has shown that, no matter whether DNA-, RNA-or methylation-based, ToO approaches are only able to resolve a subset of clinicopathologically unresolved CUPs <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">55]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, mutations in epigenetic modifiers such as ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2 could shift the distribution of somatic mutations in these cancers and reduce the reliability of RNA-or methylation-based ToO detection.

Nevertheless, a previous multi-lesion CUP case study identified a high number of fully shared mutations across all 15 metastases, found remarkably similar expression profiles, and observed distinct "galaxy"pattern evolutionary trajectories in individual CUPs [16].

text.text: Taken together, the characterized profiles suggested an occult primary in many cases but did not establish a separate biological CUP entity for the remaining tumors, especially those with low-confidence ToO prediction.
The transcriptomic analyses added another layer of heterogeneity.
We identified immuneenriched/depleted, fibrotic, and proliferative states, and these TME states were not significantly associated with other clinical or genomic features.
However, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) revealed significant associations between gene modules, histology, and genomics.
The blue module, enriched for cell-cycle and mitotic processes, was also associated with TP53 alterations, higher TMB, and neuroendocrine characteristics.

The proliferation-associated modules identified across our CUP cohort were conceptually consistent with experimental CUP models in which stem-like "agnospheres" showed growth-factorindependent proliferation, rapid multi-organ dissemination, and MAP kinase/MYC axis dependence [14].

text.text: Of note, transcriptomic analysis was also partially influenced by biopsy site, particularly through liver-associated metabolic programs.
These signals may reflect true metastatic-niche adaptation, contamination from normal tissue, or both.
Our transcriptomic analysis can not distinguish these possibilities.
But other studies have described site-specific effects in metastatic breast [56] and pancreatic cancer [57].

text.text: To investigate which genomic mechanisms might enable immune escape in CUPs, we interrogated putative GIE alterations.
They were present in 35% of tumors, most often affecting the HLA-I locus, followed by interferon-γ signaling and antigen-presentation pathways.
Notably, GIE alterations did not define the transcriptomic TME subtypes, suggesting that GIE and the overall immune state are not equivalent.
Similarly, although 61% of TMB-high tumors with RNAseq were immune-enriched, a substantial fractionwere not.

This indicates that, for CUP, high TMB does not necessarily correspond to an immune-infiltrated TME, warranting caution when applying only TMB as a biomarker for immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in CUP.
In this study, 64% of patients harbored at least one actionable alteration.
This supports the use of comprehensive molecular profiling as a way of generating new treatment options beyond empiric chemotherapy.

A recent WGS study that included an overlapping Dutch CUP population similarly reported potentially actionable alterations in 73% of CUP patients and demonstrated diagnostic and treatment utility of WGS [58].
text.formatted: A recent WGS study that included an overlapping Dutch CUP population similarly reported potentially actionable alterations in 73% of CUP patients and demonstrated diagnostic and treatment utility of WGS <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[58]</ref>.

text.text: However, the applicability of these targetable alterations is uncertain because many alteration-drug associations depend on the specific combination of alteration plus tumor type.
Therefore, further clinical trials are needed to expand the scope of tumor-agnostic alterations and therapies in CUP.
Several limitations should be mentioned.
Biopsy site and tumor purity affected bulk transcriptomes, so they cannot fully separate malignant cells from local immune, stromal, and normal tissue components.
The cohort also lacked a systematic non-CUP metastatic comparator, limiting research on CUP-specific biology.
Finally, the authors inferred actionability from retrospective molecular evidence rather than prospectively testing it.
Future studies should first specifically investigate CUP tumors that lack high-confidence ToO predictions.
Matched multi-lesion samples and single-cell or spatial profiling could be used to distinguish tumor-intrinsic signals from environmental adaptation to, or by the metastatic tissue environment.

Additionally, methylation profiling may provide complementary information to genomic and transcriptomic features, and cell-free (cfDNA) methylation has already shown feasibility for ToO prediction in CUP [10].
text.formatted: Additionally, methylation profiling may provide complementary information to genomic and transcriptomic features, and cell-free (cfDNA) methylation has already shown feasibility for ToO prediction in CUP <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: In current inconclusive CUPs, particularly when samples could be collected over time, these approaches would further help determine whether diagnostic uncertainty reflects an unusual ToO or biological changes that occur during tumor progression and metastasis.
Our integrated genomic and transcriptomic analysis provides a comprehensive, detailed view of the molecular landscape of CUP, revealing the molecular heterogeneity across CUP tumors.

While many CUP cases exhibit recognizable mutational features of established cancer types. transcriptomic profiling identified distinct immune, stromal, and proliferative states that are not fully captured by genomic subgroups or ToO predictions.
These findings demonstrate that ToO assignment alone does not fully reflect the biological complexity of CUP.

Integrating genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic data may further refine biological stratification and identify therapeutic vulnerabilities, while prospective studies are needed to establish clinical utility of multi-omics profiling.
